requirements.requirement: node3 obtains its IP address from node2's DHCP service, despite the two hosts being on different L2 segments of node1
requirements.summary: A DHCP relay (isc-dhcp-relay/dhcrelay) was installed and running on node1 bridging eth1 (toward node2) and eth2 (toward node3), forwarding broadcasts to node2's dnsmasq server at 192.168.10.10. node3 successfully obtained a real DHCP lease (192.168.20.138/139) from node2's dnsmasq, confirmed via udhcpc, dhcpcd/ifup, dnsmasq's own DHCPDISCOVER/DHCPOFFER log lines naming node3's MAC, and dnsmasq lease file entries for 'node3'.

requirements.requirement: Root cause diagnosis and correction of the return-path routing issue that prevented relay replies from reaching the client
requirements.summary: tcpdump captures on node1 showed DHCPDISCOVER reaching the relay/server but no reply returning; the executor identified the missing reverse route on node2 for the giaddr subnet (192.168.20.0/24 via node1) and added it, after which DHCPOFFER/ACK successfully reached node3.

requirements.requirement: Configuration is persistent (not just live runtime state) so DHCP relay/server/client behavior survives normal service/system restarts
requirements.summary: Static interface files (interfaces.d on node1, /etc/network/interfaces on node2/node3), sysctl.d forwarding settings, systemctl-enable of isc-dhcp-relay, rc-update-enabled dnsmasq and a boot-time route script on node2 were installed, and this persistence was independently verified by a full one-at-a-time reboot of all three nodes with automatic recovery.

requirements.requirement: Restart/recovery: for each of the three managed nodes, demonstrate healthy pre-restart baseline, a restart, a changed boot identity, and recovered relay/server/client and lease state
requirements.summary: For node1: baseline boot_id 39fdb9ab with active dhcrelay and correct addressing (cmd-cc55aeb1f67747ad), reboot acknowledged (cmd-7a711f995bca48df), transient unreachability (cmd-71cf41574e1f4366, cmd-bb2fff5b705f4bb1, cmd-82b123240b9a43ad, cmd-e27f769f072d433f), new boot_id c14f1af9 (cmd-61ac59b9a9454d4b), and recovered dhcrelay/sysctls/IPs plus a fresh downstream lease via node3 (cmd-b64d0eb1803f4dab, cmd-33f3b024ec1a490a). For node2: baseline boot_id b7edc71d with dnsmasq/route/leases (cmd-021324f2fd0b4945), reboot (cmd-ce5c55f1b6034376), new boot_id bee8f6f1 (cmd-b93e62fc6e28410c), recovered dnsmasq/route/lease file and a fresh successful lease (cmd-2df67f736b1646a4, cmd-a9954034411e4510). For node3: baseline boot_id 407511a0 with active lease (cmd-b94b62f6d490477d), reboot (cmd-512a0729b8c94280), new boot_id 4fbaa74d (cmd-684b9c6e095f4385), and automatic re-acquisition of a fresh lease with no manual intervention (cmd-4aa97ed528af4f65). Boot-identity transitions are corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots (after_executor boot IDs match the executor's own observations, and match the pre-restart values recorded in before_prepare/after_prepare).

overall_summary: The executor built a complete, correctly functioning DHCP relay chain (dnsmasq on node2, dhcrelay on node1) that lets node3 obtain its address from node2's DHCP service across node1's two isolated segments, diagnosed and fixed a real return-routing bug via packet captures, made the configuration persistent, and independently validated persistence and recovery via a full sequential reboot of all three nodes with directly observed pre-restart baselines, changed boot identities, and post-restart recovery of relay/server/client state and a fresh lease. All material task outcomes and the provider-wide restart evidence protocol are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence. Hygiene is generally good; a couple of bounded, fully-reverted troubleshooting mutations and a few leftover debug log files are the only notable deductions.
limitations: Two Alpine nodes report failed-services as unsupported (no systemctl), so any failed OpenRC services there could not be directly enumerated beyond what rc-status showed at baseline.
Leftover debug log files (/tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/node3_eth1.log, /tmp/node3_offer.log) were not explicitly confirmed as cleaned up, though they are trivial residue.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map clearly to building, diagnosing, or persisting the relay chain, and the final state on all three nodes is clean, functional, and matches the intended architecture (no failed services beyond node1's pre-existing SONiC health/watchdog units, package managers report consistent state, no unsafe broad exposure - dnsmasq and dhcrelay bind only to the intended subnet interfaces). A few bounded troubleshooting mutations occurred that were not strictly necessary and were reverted: node3's eth1 was manually given a static diagnostic IP (192.168.20.50/24) purely to ping-test the relay path (cmd-30733e18f81e4a16), later flushed by subsequent DHCP attempts; node1's isc-dhcp-relay systemd service was stopped and replaced with an ad-hoc foreground dhcrelay -d debug run (cmd-9fa5604c1970450b) before being restored to the systemd-managed service (cmd-feababfbc40744dc). Both were low-risk, fully reverted, and did not weaken any security control. Minor residue was left behind: node2 and node3 retain nohup-created log/marker files (/tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/node3_eth1.log, /tmp/node3_offer.log) visible in the after_executor temporary-files diff, which were not cleaned up but are trivial and non-sensitive.
